explanation.exam_pattern: Policy (intent) -> Standard/Baseline (mandatory) -> Procedure (steps) -> Guideline (optional advice).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Guidelines in the documentation hierarchy

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recognized desired OUTCOME of effective information security governance?

options.text: Maximizing annual security spending
Eliminating all information security risk
Achieving zero security incidents permanently
Value delivery - optimizing security investments to support business objectives

explanation.correct: Value delivery (optimizing security investment so it supports business objectives and manages risk cost-effectively) is one of governance's desired outcomes, alongside strategic alignment, risk management, resource optimization, performance measurement and assurance integration.

distractors.A: Maximizing spend is not an outcome; cost-effective value delivery is.
distractors.B: Risk is managed to an acceptable level, never fully eliminated.
distractors.C: Zero incidents is unrealistic and is not a governance outcome.

explanation.exam_pattern: Governance outcomes include strategic alignment, risk management, value delivery, resource optimization, performance measurement and assurance integration.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Desired outcomes of information security governance

questions.stem: The information security manager needs funding and senior-management commitment for a strategic security initiative. What is the BEST tool to obtain it?

options.text: A detailed technical specification of the proposed appliances
A business case expressing the initiative's risk reduction and value in business terms
A list of the security team's preferred vendors
A warning that the auditors will be upset otherwise

explanation.correct: Senior management responds to business justification: a business case that frames the initiative in terms of risk reduction, cost-benefit, and support for objectives is the manager's best instrument for buy-in and funding.

distractors.A: Technical specifications do not justify value to executives.
distractors.C: Vendor preference is not a business justification.
distractors.D: Fear of audit is a weak, negative argument compared with a value-based business case.

explanation.exam_pattern: Win senior-management support with a business case stated in business terms (risk, value, cost-benefit).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Obtaining management commitment / business case

questions.stem: After defining the current and desired states of security, the information security manager builds a roadmap. What does the roadmap PRIMARILY provide?

options.text: The organization's risk appetite statement
A sequenced, prioritized set of initiatives to move from the current state to the desired state within the organization's constraints
A catalog of every security product on the market
A guarantee that no incidents will occur

explanation.correct: The roadmap translates the strategy into a prioritized, time-sequenced plan of initiatives that closes the gap between current and desired state, respecting budget, resource and other constraints.

distractors.A: Risk appetite is set by management; it is an input to, not the output of, the roadmap.
distractors.C: A roadmap is organization-specific initiatives, not a product catalog.
distractors.D: No plan guarantees zero incidents.

explanation.exam_pattern: Roadmap = prioritized, sequenced initiatives to close the current-to-desired gap within constraints.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Strategy roadmap development

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST helps ensure the information security strategy is implemented consistently and integrates with the organization's overall technology direction?

options.text: Allowing each team to independently choose its own controls
Buying point security products as individual needs arise
A security architecture aligned with the enterprise architecture
Deferring all security decisions until after systems are built

explanation.correct: A security architecture that is derived from and aligned with the enterprise architecture gives a coherent structure so controls are consistent, integrated, and support the technology direction rather than being ad hoc.

distractors.A: Independent choices produce inconsistent, siloed controls.
distractors.B: Point purchases without an architecture create gaps and overlaps.
distractors.D: Bolting security on after build is costly and weakens integration.

explanation.exam_pattern: Security architecture (aligned to enterprise architecture) drives consistent, integrated implementation of the strategy.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Security architecture and enterprise alignment

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Senior management's visible commitment and involvement, which sets the organization's attitude toward security, is commonly called 'tone at the _____.' (one word)

explanation.correct: 'Tone at the top' describes how visible leadership support and behavior set the organizational culture and attitude toward security; it is a key governance success factor.
explanation.exam_pattern: Tone at the top = visible senior-management commitment that shapes security culture.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Tone at the top and management commitment

questions.stem: To preserve independence and avoid a conflict of interest, to whom is it generally BEST for the information security manager (CISO) to report?

options.text: The internal audit function
The network administrator
Senior management or the board (e.g., via a risk or executive committee)
The IT operations manager

explanation.correct: Reporting to senior management or the board keeps security independent of the IT functions it must oversee and gives it the authority and visibility it needs.

distractors.A: Internal audit must remain independent to audit security objectively; the CISO should not report into it.
distractors.B: A network administrator is far too low and also an operational conflict.
distractors.D: Reporting into IT operations subordinates security to operational goals and creates a conflict of interest.

explanation.exam_pattern: The CISO should report high enough (senior management/board) to stay independent of the operations it governs.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - CISO reporting line and independence

questions.stem: In a RACI chart for the security program, why should each activity have exactly ONE party designated as 'Accountable'?

options.text: Because the 'Responsible' role is unnecessary
Because only one person is ever allowed to work on the task
Because accountability can always be fully delegated to a vendor
Because accountability must be unambiguous - one party answers for the outcome and it cannot be effectively shared

explanation.correct: Accountability must rest with a single, clearly identified party so there is no confusion over who answers for the result; multiple parties may be Responsible (do the work), but accountability is singular.

distractors.A: The Responsible role (those doing the work) is still required.
distractors.B: Many people can be Responsible and perform the work; 'Accountable' is about answerability, not sole labor.
distractors.C: Operational work can be outsourced, but accountability cannot be delegated away.

explanation.exam_pattern: RACI: one Accountable per activity (answerability is singular); Responsible can be many; accountability isn't outsourced.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - RACI and accountability

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following are GOVERNANCE responsibilities of the board and senior management rather than the information security manager? (Choose two.)

options.text: Performing hands-on forensic analysis during an incident
Configuring and maintaining firewall rule sets
Providing visible support and adequate resources for the security program
Approving the organization's risk appetite

explanation.correct: Setting/approving risk appetite and providing visible support and resources are board/senior-management governance duties; the manager and specialists execute within that direction.

distractors.A: Hands-on forensics is performed by specialists, not the board or senior management.
distractors.B: Firewall configuration is an operational task performed by technical staff, not a governance duty.

explanation.exam_pattern: Board/senior mgmt: set risk appetite, give support/resources, oversee; they do not perform operational/technical tasks.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Governance vs operational responsibilities

questions.stem: Who is PRIMARILY responsible for ensuring that employees within a business unit follow information security policies in their day-to-day work?

options.text: The external auditors
The data custodians in IT
That business unit's line management (its managers)
The information security manager personally

explanation.correct: Line managers are responsible for enforcing policy and secure behavior within their own units; security is embedded in the business, not policed solely by the security team.

distractors.A: Auditors independently assess compliance; they do not enforce it operationally.
distractors.B: Custodians maintain technical controls; they do not supervise staff behavior.
distractors.D: The security manager sets direction and facilitates but cannot personally enforce behavior in every unit.

explanation.exam_pattern: Line/business management enforces policy within its own area; security facilitates, audit assures.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Line management responsibility for compliance

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: An independent function that provides the board with assurance on whether security controls are operating effectively, without owning or running them, is internal _____. (one word)

explanation.correct: Internal audit provides independent assurance over control effectiveness; keeping it independent of the functions it audits is essential to objective oversight.
explanation.exam_pattern: Internal audit = independent assurance; it must not own or run the controls it evaluates.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Internal audit and independent assurance

questions.stem: An organization is expanding into several countries, each with its own data-protection laws. What should the information security manager do FIRST?

options.text: Apply only the home country's laws everywhere
Identify all applicable legal and regulatory requirements across the jurisdictions involved
Immediately adopt the controls used by the largest competitor
Halt the expansion to avoid any compliance work

explanation.correct: The manager must first determine which laws and regulations apply in each jurisdiction; you cannot design compliant controls before you know the obligations.

distractors.A: Other jurisdictions' laws still apply to activities there.
distractors.C: Copying a competitor ignores the organization's own obligations and context.
distractors.D: Halting expansion is a disproportionate overreaction, not a risk-based first step.

explanation.exam_pattern: Multi-jurisdiction: FIRST identify all applicable requirements, then harmonize and design controls.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Identifying applicable legal/regulatory requirements

questions.stem: Having investigated its risks (due diligence), an organization then takes reasonable, ongoing measures a prudent organization would take to protect its assets. This ongoing action is BEST described as:

options.text: Risk acceptance
Risk avoidance
Due diligence
Due care

explanation.correct: Due care is the ongoing, prudent action taken to protect assets - the 'doing' that follows the investigation (due diligence).

distractors.A: Risk acceptance is a specific treatment decision, not the general duty of prudent care.
distractors.B: Risk avoidance eliminates an activity; it is not the general duty of care.
distractors.C: Due diligence is the prior investigation/evaluation, not the ongoing protective action.

explanation.exam_pattern: Due diligence = investigate beforehand; due care = act prudently and continuously afterward.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Due care versus due diligence

questions.stem: A new privacy law gives individuals the right to request erasure of their personal data. What should the information security manager do FIRST to prepare the organization to comply?

options.text: Announce publicly that the organization cannot comply
Identify and map where personal data is collected, stored, and processed
Delete the entire customer database immediately
Purchase encryption software for all servers

explanation.correct: You cannot honor an erasure (or any data-subject) request without first knowing where the personal data resides; data discovery/mapping is the necessary first step.

distractors.A: Declaring non-compliance before assessing the situation is premature and harmful.
distractors.C: Deleting all data destroys information the business legitimately needs - an overreaction.
distractors.D: Buying encryption is technology-first and does not address knowing where data lives or enabling erasure.

explanation.exam_pattern: New privacy obligation -> FIRST inventory/map personal data, then build the process to meet the requirement.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Privacy requirements and data mapping

questions.stem: A jurisdiction requires organizations to notify regulators of qualifying data breaches within a set time. What should the information security manager ensure is in place to meet this obligation?

options.text: A policy never to report breaches to anyone
Full reliance on the cloud provider to handle all legal obligations
A plan to notify only if the media discovers the breach
A defined breach-notification process aligned with the legal timelines and integrated into the incident response plan

explanation.correct: Meeting a legal notification deadline requires a pre-defined process (who decides, who is notified, within what timeframe) built into the incident response plan so the organization can act within the mandated window.

distractors.A: Never reporting violates the law.
distractors.B: Legal accountability cannot be outsourced to a provider.
distractors.C: Waiting for media exposure is evasive and still breaches the legal deadline.

explanation.exam_pattern: Know the obligation in advance and bake breach-notification timelines into the IR plan.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Breach-notification obligations

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The legal principle that senior managers can be held liable if they fail to exercise the care a reasonable individual would exercise in protecting the organization is known as the 'prudent _____ rule.' (one word)

explanation.correct: Under the prudent-person rule, officers must act with the diligence and care a reasonable (prudent) person would in the same situation; failing to do so can create personal liability - a key driver of due care.
explanation.exam_pattern: Prudent-person rule = act as a reasonable person would; underpins due care and management liability.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 1 - Prudent-person rule and liability

questions.stem: A data-center asset is valued at $200,000. A flood would destroy an estimated 25% of its value, and floods are expected about once every 10 years. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE)?

explanation.correct: SLE = asset value x exposure factor = $200,000 x 0.25 = $50,000. ALE = SLE x ARO = $50,000 x 0.1 (once per 10 years) = $5,000.

distractors.A: $50,000 is the single loss expectancy (SLE); it omits the annualized rate of occurrence.
distractors.C: $20,000 multiplies asset value by ARO but wrongly omits the exposure factor.
distractors.D: $500 reflects a misplaced decimal in the ARO.

explanation.exam_pattern: SLE = AV x EF; ALE = SLE x ARO. Watch for answers that drop the EF or the ARO.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Quantitative risk analysis (SLE, ARO, ALE)

questions.stem: A risk analysis rates each risk's likelihood and impact as 'High,' 'Medium,' or 'Low' instead of calculating monetary values. This approach is BEST described as:

options.text: A penetration test
Quantitative risk analysis
A business impact analysis
Qualitative risk analysis

explanation.correct: Qualitative analysis uses descriptive/relative ratings (High/Medium/Low) rather than numeric monetary values; it is faster but less precise than quantitative analysis.

distractors.A: A penetration test is a hands-on technical assessment, not a risk-rating method.
distractors.B: Quantitative analysis assigns numeric/monetary values (e.g., SLE, ALE).
distractors.C: A BIA assesses the impact of disruptions on business processes for continuity planning.

explanation.exam_pattern: Qualitative = High/Medium/Low ratings; quantitative = numeric/monetary (SLE, ALE).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Qualitative versus quantitative analysis

questions.stem: When is it BEST to perform a risk assessment for a major new system?

options.text: Only at the very end of the system's life
Before deployment (during design/selection) and again after significant changes
Never, provided the vendor is reputable
Only after a breach has occurred

explanation.correct: Assessing risk before deployment lets the organization design in appropriate controls, and reassessing after significant change keeps the picture current - risk management is proactive and continuous.

distractors.A: Assessing only at end-of-life provides no protection during operation.
distractors.C: Vendor reputation is not a substitute for assessing the organization's own risk.
distractors.D: Waiting for a breach is reactive and too late to prevent avoidable harm.

explanation.exam_pattern: Assess risk before deployment and after significant change - proactive, not reactive.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Timing of risk assessments

questions.stem: A disgruntled administrator who could abuse privileged access is BEST described, in risk terminology, as a:

options.text: Threat (threat source/agent)
Vulnerability
Control
Residual risk

explanation.correct: A threat (source/agent) is the potential cause of an unwanted event; a disgruntled insider with the means and motive to misuse access is a threat agent.

distractors.B: A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat exploits (e.g., excessive privileges), not the actor.
distractors.C: A control reduces risk; it is not the threat.
distractors.D: Residual risk is the exposure remaining after controls, not the actor.

explanation.exam_pattern: Threat (agent) = potential cause; vulnerability = weakness it exploits; risk = likelihood/impact of exploitation.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Threat sources and agents

questions.stem: When estimating the LIKELIHOOD that a vulnerability will be exploited, which factor is MOST relevant?

options.text: The book value of the affected asset
The capability and motivation of threat actors combined with how easily the vulnerability can be exploited
The number of employees in the organization
The total size of the security budget

explanation.correct: Likelihood depends on the threat (capability and motivation) and the ease of exploiting the weakness (including whether an exploit exists and the exposure).

distractors.A: Asset value affects the impact side of risk, not the likelihood of exploitation.
distractors.C: Headcount does not determine how likely a given vulnerability is to be exploited.
distractors.D: Budget size influences control capacity, not the inherent likelihood of an exploit.

explanation.exam_pattern: Likelihood = threat capability/motivation x ease of exploitation; asset value drives impact, not likelihood.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Estimating likelihood

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Single loss expectancy (SLE) equals the asset value multiplied by the _____ factor, which represents the proportion of the asset lost in a single event. (one word)

explanation.correct: SLE = asset value x exposure factor (EF). The EF is the percentage of asset value lost in a single occurrence of the threat.
explanation.exam_pattern: SLE = AV x EF; ALE = SLE x ARO. EF is the fraction of value lost per event.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Exposure factor and SLE

questions.stem: To reduce the likelihood and impact of account compromise, the organization implements multi-factor authentication and network segmentation. Which risk response does this represent?

options.text: Mitigation (risk reduction)
Transfer (sharing)
Avoidance
Acceptance

explanation.correct: Applying controls to lower a risk's likelihood or impact is mitigation (risk reduction) - the most common response.

distractors.B: Transfer shifts the loss to a third party (e.g., insurance), not reduce it with controls.
distractors.C: Avoidance eliminates the activity that creates the risk.
distractors.D: Acceptance takes no action and retains the risk.

explanation.exam_pattern: Controls that lower likelihood/impact = mitigation; the four responses are mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Risk mitigation

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes the difference between risk appetite and risk tolerance?

options.text: Risk appetite is always zero, while tolerance is unlimited

Risk appetite is the broad amount of risk the organization is willing to take to meet its objectives; risk tolerance is the acceptable deviation around that level, usually expressed as specific, measurable thresholds
They are identical terms with no practical difference
Risk tolerance is set only by the security team without management input

explanation.correct: Appetite is the strategic, broad level of risk the organization will pursue; tolerance is the tactical, acceptable deviation around that level, typically stated as measurable thresholds that KRIs monitor.

distractors.A: Appetite is rarely zero, and tolerance is not unlimited; both are bounded by objectives.
distractors.C: They are related but distinct - one is broad/strategic, the other specific/tactical.
distractors.D: Both appetite and tolerance are management/board decisions, not set by the security team alone.

explanation.exam_pattern: Appetite = broad strategic level of acceptable risk; tolerance = acceptable, measurable deviation around it.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Risk appetite versus risk tolerance

questions.stem: A risk is found to EXCEED the organization's risk appetite. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate for the information security manager? (Choose two.)

options.text: Remove the risk from tracking to avoid alarming management
Record the risk and its status in the risk register
Present risk treatment options to the risk owner/management for a decision
Unilaterally accept the risk on the organization's behalf

explanation.correct: When a risk exceeds appetite, the manager escalates with treatment options for the risk owner to decide and documents the risk and its status in the register - facilitating a management decision, not making it alone.

distractors.A: Hiding the risk removes visibility management needs to decide.
distractors.D: The manager does not own or accept business risk; acceptance is management's decision.

explanation.exam_pattern: Over-appetite risk -> manager escalates options to the risk owner and documents it; management decides.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Escalating risks beyond appetite

questions.stem: An organization transfers risk by buying cyber-insurance and outsourcing security monitoring. Which statement is TRUE about what has actually been transferred?

options.text: The financial or operational burden may shift, but accountability for the risk and the data remains with the organization
The risk can now be deleted from the risk register
No further monitoring of the arrangement is required
All accountability moves permanently to the insurer and the provider

explanation.correct: Transfer shifts some financial or operational burden to a third party, but the organization remains accountable for the risk and its data; transfer is not a way to offload accountability.

distractors.B: The risk remains and must still be tracked.
distractors.C: Outsourced/insured arrangements require ongoing monitoring of the third party.
distractors.D: Accountability cannot be transferred away by contract or insurance.

explanation.exam_pattern: You can transfer financial/operational burden, not accountability; keep monitoring the arrangement.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Limits of risk transfer

questions.stem: Management has decided to mitigate a high risk by implementing new controls. What should the information security manager prepare to guide and track that mitigation?

options.text: A decision to accept the risk instead
A new company-wide holiday schedule
A press release announcing the risk
A risk treatment (action) plan with assigned owners, actions, and target dates

explanation.correct: A risk treatment/action plan documents the chosen controls, responsible owners, actions, and timelines so implementation can be driven and tracked to completion.

distractors.A: Accepting the risk contradicts management's decision to mitigate.
distractors.B: A holiday schedule has nothing to do with risk treatment.
distractors.C: A press release is unrelated to implementing controls.

explanation.exam_pattern: Chosen mitigation is implemented and tracked via a risk treatment/action plan (owners, actions, dates).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Risk treatment plans

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Knowingly taking no further action and retaining a risk whose exposure is within the organization's risk appetite is risk _____. (one word)

explanation.correct: Risk acceptance is the informed decision to retain a risk (take no further mitigation), appropriate when the residual exposure is within appetite and formally approved by the risk owner.
explanation.exam_pattern: Acceptance = informed retention of a risk within appetite, formally approved by management.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Risk acceptance

questions.stem: A key risk indicator (KRI) crosses its predefined threshold, signaling rising exposure. What should the information security manager do FIRST?

options.text: Delete the KRI so it stops generating alerts
Immediately shut down all business systems
Wait until the next annual review to look into it
Investigate the cause and report the changed exposure to the risk owner for a decision

explanation.correct: A breached KRI threshold is an early warning: the manager analyzes the cause and reports the changed exposure to the risk owner so an informed treatment decision can be made.

distractors.A: Deleting the KRI suppresses the warning it was designed to provide.
distractors.B: Shutting everything down is disproportionate before the cause is understood.
distractors.C: Waiting defeats the purpose of an early-warning indicator.

explanation.exam_pattern: KRI threshold breached -> investigate and escalate to the risk owner; it is an early warning, not an automatic shutdown.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Acting on KRI thresholds

questions.stem: What MOST determines whether a metric is an effective key risk indicator (KRI)?

options.text: It is expressed only in deep technical jargon
It is a relevant, measurable leading indicator that reliably signals changes in risk exposure against a threshold
It is simply the easiest number for the team to collect
It always trends upward over time

explanation.correct: A good KRI is relevant to a specific risk, measurable, and predictive (leading) - it warns of changing exposure against a defined threshold so management can act early.

distractors.A: Jargon-heavy metrics are less useful; KRIs should be understandable to decision-makers.
distractors.C: Ease of collection does not make a metric a meaningful predictor of risk.
distractors.D: A KRI need not always rise; it must reflect actual changes in exposure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Effective KRI = relevant, measurable, leading/predictive, tied to a threshold.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Designing effective KRIs

questions.stem: Why should the information security manager consider risk AGGREGATION when reviewing the risk register?

options.text: Several individually minor but related risks can combine into an aggregate risk that exceeds the organization's appetite
Aggregation always reduces the total level of risk
It allows unrelated risks to be deleted in bulk
It removes the need to assign risk owners

explanation.correct: Risks that look minor in isolation can, when combined or correlated, produce a much larger aggregate exposure that breaches appetite; aggregation ensures these are seen and managed.

distractors.B: Aggregation typically reveals a larger combined exposure, not a smaller one.
distractors.C: Aggregation is about combined exposure, not bulk deletion.
distractors.D: Risk owners are still required regardless of aggregation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Aggregate related 'small' risks - combined they can exceed appetite even when each alone does not.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Risk aggregation

questions.stem: Which event should MOST prompt the information security manager to update the organization's risk register?

options.text: A significant business or environmental change, such as a merger, a new product line, or a major breach affecting the industry
A change to the office lunch menu
The hiring of a new receptionist
A routine, scheduled password reset

explanation.correct: Material changes to the business or threat environment can create, remove, or alter risks, so they should trigger an update to the register in addition to periodic review.

distractors.B: A lunch-menu change has no effect on the risk profile.
distractors.C: A routine non-sensitive hire does not materially change enterprise risk.
distractors.D: A routine password reset is business as usual, not a risk-changing event.

explanation.exam_pattern: Update the register on significant business/environmental change, not just on a fixed calendar.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Triggers for risk reassessment

questions.stem: What is the BEST way to keep senior management informed of the organization's information security risk status over time?

options.text: Provide regular, consistent risk reporting (e.g., a risk dashboard or updated register) highlighting trends and items outside appetite
Forward raw vulnerability-scan output files whenever they are produced
Avoid reporting risk to prevent alarming the board
Report on risk only after a serious incident has occurred

explanation.correct: Consistent, business-oriented risk reporting - trends, status against appetite, key items - gives management the ongoing visibility it needs to make informed decisions.

distractors.B: Raw scan files are too technical and not decision-useful for management.
distractors.C: Withholding risk information prevents informed governance.
distractors.D: Reporting only after incidents is reactive and leaves management blind in between.

explanation.exam_pattern: Give management regular, trend-based risk reporting tied to appetite - not raw data or silence.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Risk reporting to management

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The ongoing process of tracking identified risks, control effectiveness and the threat environment so that risk decisions stay current is risk _____. (one word)

explanation.correct: Risk monitoring is the continuous tracking of risks, control performance, and the environment, enabling timely reassessment and reporting as conditions change.
explanation.exam_pattern: Risk monitoring = continuous tracking that keeps the risk picture and decisions current.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Risk monitoring

questions.stem: After information has been classified, what MOST ensures it is protected consistently throughout its lifecycle?

options.text: Letting each employee decide how to handle the data
A single firewall at the network perimeter
Automatically deleting all classified data after one week
Defined handling, labeling, and storage requirements for each classification level

explanation.correct: Classification only drives protection if each level has defined handling, labeling, and storage rules; these make consistent, commensurate protection actionable across the data lifecycle.

distractors.A: Letting everyone improvise produces inconsistent, non-compliant handling.
distractors.B: A perimeter firewall is one control and does not govern handling across the lifecycle.
distractors.C: Blanket deletion is not a handling scheme and destroys needed data.

explanation.exam_pattern: Classification must be paired with handling/labeling standards per level to drive consistent protection.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Data handling and labeling

questions.stem: A hospital's PRIMARY concern for its patient medication records is that they not be altered without authorization. When classifying this data, which security attribute is the primary driver?

options.text: Integrity
Confidentiality
Scalability
Availability

explanation.correct: The stated concern is unauthorized alteration, which is an integrity issue; classification should ensure controls that protect accuracy and prevent unauthorized change.

distractors.B: Confidentiality concerns unauthorized disclosure, not alteration.
distractors.C: Scalability is a performance attribute, not a security property.
distractors.D: Availability concerns access/uptime, not unauthorized change.

explanation.exam_pattern: Map the stated concern to CIA: alteration = integrity; disclosure = confidentiality; uptime/access = availability.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Classification and the CIA triad

questions.stem: Individually, several data fields are low sensitivity, but combined they can identify individuals and reveal their health status. How should this affect classification?

options.text: Aggregation never changes the sensitivity of data
Classification should always follow only the single least-sensitive field
The data should be made public to simplify handling
The combined dataset may warrant a higher classification than its individual fields, because of aggregation

explanation.correct: Aggregation can raise sensitivity: combining individually innocuous fields may enable identification or reveal sensitive attributes, so the combined dataset can justify a higher classification.

distractors.A: Aggregation can materially increase sensitivity through inference.
distractors.B: Classifying by the least-sensitive field understates the real sensitivity of the aggregate.
distractors.C: Making sensitive aggregated data public is reckless.

explanation.exam_pattern: Aggregation can raise classification - combined low-sensitivity data may become sensitive.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Aggregation and classification

questions.stem: What should trigger a review of an information asset's classification level?

options.text: A change in the company's stock ticker symbol
Only the eventual retirement of the asset
A change in the asset's value, sensitivity, or regulatory status, in addition to periodic review
Nothing - a classification is permanent once assigned

explanation.correct: Sensitivity changes over time (e.g., data becomes public, or new regulation applies), so classification should be reviewed periodically and whenever the asset's value, sensitivity, or regulatory status changes.

distractors.A: A ticker-symbol change does not affect data sensitivity.
distractors.B: Retirement is one trigger but far too narrow on its own.
distractors.D: Classification is not permanent; it must be revisited as sensitivity changes.

explanation.exam_pattern: Reclassify on change in value/sensitivity/regulation and on periodic review - classification is not static.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Reviewing classification over time

questions.stem: When designing a data classification scheme, what is a key BEST practice regarding the NUMBER of classification levels?

options.text: Create as many levels as possible for maximum granularity
Use the fewest levels necessary so the scheme is simple enough to be applied consistently
Use exactly one level for all data in the organization
Let each department invent its own incompatible set of levels

explanation.correct: A workable scheme uses the fewest levels needed to distinguish protection requirements; too many levels become confusing and are applied inconsistently, undermining the whole scheme.

distractors.A: Excessive granularity is impractical and leads to inconsistent classification.
distractors.C: A single level cannot distinguish differing protection needs.
distractors.D: Incompatible per-department schemes destroy consistency and interoperability.

explanation.exam_pattern: Keep the classification scheme simple (few, clear levels) so it is applied consistently.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Designing a classification scheme

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Assigning a sensitivity level such as 'Confidential' or 'Public' to information so that commensurate controls can be applied is called data _____. (one word)

explanation.correct: Data classification assigns a sensitivity level to information so that protection can be applied in proportion to its value and sensitivity.
explanation.exam_pattern: Classification = assigning sensitivity levels so controls match the data's value/sensitivity.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 2 - Data classification

questions.stem: Two proposed initiatives would reduce similar amounts of risk, but one costs far less than the other. From a CISM perspective, which should the information security manager prioritize, and why?

options.text: The higher-cost initiative, because higher spending always means better security
Neither, because cost should never influence a security decision
Whichever initiative the newest vendor is promoting
The lower-cost initiative, because it delivers greater value and optimizes limited resources

explanation.correct: With comparable risk reduction, the lower-cost option provides greater value and makes better use of scarce resources - resource optimization and value delivery are core program objectives.

distractors.A: Spending more does not linearly improve security and ignores cost-benefit.
distractors.B: Cost-effectiveness is central to program decisions; cost must be considered.
distractors.C: Vendor promotion is not a basis for prioritization.

explanation.exam_pattern: Equal risk reduction -> choose the more cost-effective option (value delivery, resource optimization).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Resource optimization and value

questions.stem: A business unit complains that security 'slows them down.' What is the BEST way for the information security manager to position the security program?

options.text: As a business enabler that manages risk so the business can pursue its objectives safely, engaging with the unit early
As a gatekeeper whose main job is to say 'no' to new initiatives
As an obstacle the business simply has to tolerate
As a purely technical function with no need for business involvement

explanation.correct: Security should be framed and run as a business enabler: by managing risk and engaging early, it helps the business move faster and more safely, which also builds support for the program.

distractors.B: A 'department of no' creates friction and gets bypassed.
distractors.C: Positioning security as an obstacle undermines its own effectiveness.
distractors.D: Security divorced from the business cannot align with objectives.

explanation.exam_pattern: Position security as a business enabler (manage risk, engage early), not a blocker.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Security as a business enabler

questions.stem: At what point is it MOST cost-effective to incorporate security requirements into a new application?

options.text: Never, since developers will handle it informally
After the application is already in production
Early, during the requirements and design phases of the development lifecycle
Only once a vulnerability has been exploited

explanation.correct: Building security in from requirements/design is far cheaper and more effective than retrofitting it; defects found late cost much more to fix (security by design).

distractors.A: Leaving it to informal handling produces inconsistent, weak controls.
distractors.B: Adding security after go-live means costly rework and residual exposure.
distractors.D: Waiting for exploitation is reactive and damaging.

explanation.exam_pattern: Build security in early (requirements/design) - the SDLC is where it is cheapest and most effective.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Security in the SDLC

questions.stem: The information security strategy sets direction. What does the information security PROGRAM primarily provide?

options.text: The organization's risk appetite
The execution - the projects, controls, resources, and processes that implement the strategy
The board's governance charter
The external auditor's independent opinion

explanation.correct: The program is the execution vehicle: it delivers the initiatives, controls, people, and processes that turn the strategy's direction into operational reality.

distractors.A: Risk appetite is set by the board/senior management, not produced by the program.
distractors.C: A governance charter is a governance artifact, not the program.
distractors.D: The auditor's opinion is independent assurance, separate from the program.

explanation.exam_pattern: Strategy = direction; program = execution (projects, controls, resources, processes).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Program as execution of the strategy

questions.stem: Before rolling out specific technical controls under a new security program, what should the information security manager ensure is approved to give those controls their authority?

options.text: A new corporate brand logo
The procurement team's travel budget
A list of competitor tools
Information security policies (and supporting standards) approved by management

explanation.correct: Controls derive their mandate from management-approved policies and standards; establishing that authority first makes the controls enforceable and defensible.

distractors.A: A logo has nothing to do with control authority.
distractors.B: A travel budget is unrelated to the program's mandate.
distractors.C: A competitor tool list does not authorize the organization's controls.

explanation.exam_pattern: Controls get their authority from approved policies/standards - establish those first.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Policies as the foundation for controls

questions.stem: To prevent security from being unintentionally weakened when systems are modified, security review should be embedded in which process?

options.text: Change management
Payroll processing
Office space planning
The annual holiday calendar

explanation.correct: Embedding security review in the change-management process ensures modifications are assessed for security impact and approved before implementation, preventing drift and unmanaged risk.

distractors.B: Payroll is unrelated to securing system changes.
distractors.C: Office space planning does not govern system modifications.
distractors.D: A holiday calendar has no bearing on change security.

explanation.exam_pattern: Integrate security into change management so modifications are risk-assessed and approved.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Security in change management

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Designing systems and processes so that security is built in from the outset rather than added later is known as security by _____. (one word)

explanation.correct: Security by design embeds security into architecture and development from the start, which is more effective and cheaper than retrofitting controls later.
explanation.exam_pattern: Security by design = build security in from the start (cheaper, stronger than bolt-on).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Security by design

questions.stem: Restoring affected systems from clean backups after a ransomware attack is an example of which functional control type?

options.text: Detective
Corrective
Preventive
Deterrent

explanation.correct: A corrective control restores systems/operations after an incident - recovering from backup is a classic corrective (recovery) action.

distractors.A: Detective controls identify that an event occurred (e.g., alerts), not restore service.
distractors.C: Preventive controls stop an event before it happens.
distractors.D: Deterrent controls discourage an action (e.g., a warning banner).

explanation.exam_pattern: Restore/repair after an event = corrective; prevent = before; detect = find; deter = discourage.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Control types (corrective)

questions.stem: A login banner warning that systems are monitored and that unauthorized use will be prosecuted is BEST classified as which control type?

options.text: Recovery
Compensating
Deterrent
Corrective

explanation.correct: A deterrent control discourages a would-be actor from attempting an action; a warning banner is intended to dissuade misuse.

distractors.A: Recovery controls restore operations after disruption.
distractors.B: A compensating control substitutes for an infeasible primary control.
distractors.D: Corrective controls fix or restore after an event.

explanation.exam_pattern: Warning banner/signage = deterrent (discourages the act before it happens).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Control types (deterrent)

questions.stem: Granting each user only the access rights required to perform their job duties implements which principle?

options.text: Implicit allow
Defense in depth
Least privilege
Security through obscurity

explanation.correct: Least privilege limits each user's access to only what is needed for their role, reducing the attack surface and the impact of compromise or misuse.

distractors.A: Implicit allow is the opposite of good practice; default-deny is preferred.
distractors.B: Defense in depth is about layering multiple controls, not limiting individual access.
distractors.D: Security through obscurity relies on secrecy of design, not on restricting access.

explanation.exam_pattern: Minimum access needed for the job = least privilege.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Least privilege

questions.stem: A process is designed so that no single individual can both initiate and approve the same financial transaction. Which control principle does this implement?

options.text: Single sign-on
Job rotation
Separation (segregation) of duties
Least privilege

explanation.correct: Separation of duties divides a sensitive task among people so that no one person can complete it alone, reducing fraud and error.

distractors.A: Single sign-on is an authentication convenience, not a duty-splitting control.
distractors.B: Job rotation moves staff between roles to detect/deter fraud; it is a different control.
distractors.D: Least privilege limits access scope but does not by itself split a transaction across people.

explanation.exam_pattern: No single person completes a sensitive transaction = separation/segregation of duties.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Separation of duties

questions.stem: Deploying multiple, overlapping layers of controls so that the failure of any one layer does not immediately expose the asset is BEST described as:

options.text: Risk acceptance
Defense in depth (layered security)
A single point of failure
Security through obscurity

explanation.correct: Defense in depth layers independent controls so that if one fails, others still protect the asset - redundancy that improves resilience.

distractors.A: Risk acceptance is a treatment decision, not a layering strategy.
distractors.C: A single point of failure is the opposite - one failure causes full exposure.
distractors.D: Security through obscurity relies on secrecy, not layered controls.

explanation.exam_pattern: Overlapping, independent layers = defense in depth.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Defense in depth

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following are technical (logical) controls? (Choose two.)

options.text: A security awareness poster in the break room
Encryption of data at rest
A visitor sign-in sheet at reception
Multi-factor authentication

explanation.correct: Encryption and multi-factor authentication are technical (logical) controls implemented in systems/software.

distractors.A: An awareness poster is an administrative/awareness control.
distractors.C: A visitor sign-in sheet is a physical/administrative control at the premises.

explanation.exam_pattern: Technical = implemented in systems (encryption, MFA, ACLs); administrative = policy/training; physical = premises.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Technical control category

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Controls are grouped into three categories by their nature: technical, physical, and _____ (managerial). (one word)

explanation.correct: The three control categories are technical (logical), physical, and administrative (managerial) - the people/process controls such as policies, procedures, and training.
explanation.exam_pattern: Control categories: technical, physical, administrative (managerial).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Control categories

questions.stem: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 introduced a new core function covering organizational context, risk-management strategy, roles, policy, and oversight. Which function is it?

options.text: Protect
Recover
Respond
Govern

explanation.correct: CSF 2.0 added Govern as a sixth core function, emphasizing governance, risk strategy, roles/responsibilities, and policy that cut across the other five functions.

distractors.A: Protect (safeguards) was already a core function in CSF 1.1.
distractors.B: Recover (restoration) was already present in CSF 1.1.
distractors.C: Respond (acting on detected incidents) was already present in CSF 1.1.

explanation.exam_pattern: CSF 2.0 functions: Govern (new), Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - NIST CSF 2.0 Govern function

questions.stem: Which publication provides a comprehensive catalog of security and privacy controls widely used by U.S. federal agencies and their contractors?

options.text: PCI DSS
ITIL
ISO/IEC 27014
NIST SP 800-53

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-53 is a detailed catalog of security and privacy controls, extensively used across U.S. federal systems and beyond.

distractors.A: PCI DSS is a payment-card data security standard, not a general control catalog.
distractors.B: ITIL is an IT service-management framework, not a security control catalog.
distractors.C: ISO/IEC 27014 addresses the governance of information security, not a control catalog.

explanation.exam_pattern: Comprehensive control catalog (US federal) = NIST SP 800-53.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - NIST SP 800-53 control catalog

questions.stem: An organization stores and processes credit-card data. Which standard applies MOST directly to that activity?

options.text: PCI DSS
NIST Cybersecurity Framework
COBIT

explanation.correct: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) directly governs the handling of cardholder data.

distractors.B: ISO 22301 is a business-continuity management standard.
distractors.C: The NIST CSF is a voluntary cybersecurity framework, not the card-data mandate.
distractors.D: COBIT is an enterprise IT governance framework, not a card-data standard.

explanation.exam_pattern: Cardholder data = PCI DSS applies most directly.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - PCI DSS applicability

questions.stem: What is the PRIMARY benefit of adopting an established security control framework rather than building controls ad hoc?

options.text: It guarantees the organization can never be breached
It removes the need to perform a risk assessment
It eliminates the need for management involvement
It provides a structured, comprehensive, recognized baseline that reduces gaps and supports consistency and benchmarking

explanation.correct: A recognized framework gives a complete, structured starting point so controls are comprehensive and consistent, gaps are reduced, and the program can be benchmarked and assured.

distractors.A: No framework guarantees breach immunity.
distractors.B: Frameworks are applied on a risk basis; they do not replace risk assessment.
distractors.C: Management involvement remains essential to governance and resourcing.

explanation.exam_pattern: Frameworks give a structured, comprehensive, benchmarkable baseline - not a breach guarantee.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Value of control frameworks

questions.stem: When selecting a security framework or control set, what should MOST influence the choice?

options.text: The organization's business objectives, regulatory requirements, and risk profile
Whichever framework has the longest name
Whatever framework is cheapest to download
The personal preference of a single engineer

explanation.correct: The right framework is the one that fits the organization's context - its objectives, the regulations it must meet, and its risk profile - not a generic or arbitrary choice.

distractors.B: A name's length is irrelevant.
distractors.C: Download cost is trivial compared with fit-for-purpose.
distractors.D: One engineer's preference is not a sound organizational basis.

explanation.exam_pattern: Choose a framework for fit: business objectives, regulatory needs, and risk profile.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Selecting an appropriate framework

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The ISO/IEC standard that provides guidance specifically on information security risk management, supporting an ISMS, is ISO/IEC _____. (enter the number)

explanation.correct: ISO/IEC 27005 gives guidance on information security risk management, complementing the ISMS requirements of ISO/IEC 27001 and the controls of ISO/IEC 27002.
explanation.exam_pattern: 27001 = ISMS requirements; 27002 = controls; 27005 = risk management; 27014 = governance.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - ISO/IEC 27005 risk management

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes security 'awareness' from security 'training'?

options.text: They are the same thing with different names
Awareness changes attitudes and keeps security top-of-mind across the workforce, while training teaches specific skills needed to perform tasks securely
Awareness is only for IT and training is only for executives
Training is a one-time poster and awareness is a professional certification

explanation.correct: Awareness focuses general attention and attitudes so people recognize risks; training builds specific job skills (e.g., secure coding). They are complementary, not identical.

distractors.A: They differ in purpose and depth - broad attitude change versus specific skills.
distractors.C: Both apply across the workforce, not to narrow audiences.
distractors.D: This mischaracterizes both; a poster is an awareness tactic, not training.

explanation.exam_pattern: Awareness = attention/attitude (broad); training = specific skills to perform tasks securely.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Awareness versus training

questions.stem: Developers need secure-coding training while finance staff need to recognize payment fraud. This difference illustrates the need for security education that is:

options.text: Delivered only once at hire
Identical for every employee
Role-based (tailored to job responsibilities)
Limited to the security team

explanation.correct: Different roles face different risks, so role-based education targets the content each group actually needs, making it relevant and effective.

distractors.A: One-time-at-hire training is not sufficient or ongoing.
distractors.B: One-size-fits-all content ignores role-specific risks.
distractors.D: Education must reach the whole workforce, not just the security team.

explanation.exam_pattern: Different roles, different risks -> role-based training.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Role-based security education

questions.stem: When should security awareness education BEST be delivered to employees?

options.text: At onboarding and then reinforced periodically and whenever significant changes occur
Only during the annual financial audit
Never, to avoid distracting staff
Only after an employee has caused an incident

explanation.correct: Awareness should start at onboarding and be reinforced on an ongoing basis (and on relevant change) so it stays current and shapes a lasting security culture.

distractors.B: Tying awareness to the audit cycle is arbitrary and insufficient.
distractors.C: Skipping awareness leaves the workforce vulnerable.
distractors.D: Training only after an incident is reactive and too late.

explanation.exam_pattern: Awareness is continuous: at onboarding and reinforced periodically and on change.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Timing and frequency of awareness

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST indicates that an organization has a strong security culture?

options.text: Employees proactively report suspicious activity and follow policy without needing to be compelled
Only the security team is aware of the policies
Staff routinely share passwords to work faster
Employees never mention or think about security at all

explanation.correct: A strong culture shows in behavior: people proactively report concerns and follow policy because they value security, not merely because they are forced to.

distractors.B: Policies known only to the security team indicate poor awareness.
distractors.C: Password sharing is insecure behavior, the opposite of a strong culture.
distractors.D: Silence/apathy signals a weak culture, not a strong one.

explanation.exam_pattern: Strong culture = proactive reporting and voluntary policy adherence.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Security culture indicators

questions.stem: What is the PRIMARY purpose of running simulated phishing campaigns against employees?

options.text: To satisfy a request from the marketing department
To identify and punish individual employees
To measure susceptibility and improve behavior through targeted follow-up training
To replace all email-filtering technology

explanation.correct: Phishing simulations are a measurement-and-improvement tool: they gauge resilience and direct targeted training, strengthening behavior over time.

distractors.A: They serve security objectives, not marketing.
distractors.B: Using simulations punitively undermines trust and reporting.
distractors.D: Simulations do not replace technical email controls.

explanation.exam_pattern: Phishing simulations measure and improve behavior (training), not punish staff or replace controls.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Phishing simulations

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Security _____ programs aim to change employee behavior and build a security-conscious culture across the entire workforce. (one word)

explanation.correct: Security awareness programs seek to change behavior and build a security-conscious culture, complementing (not replacing) technical controls.
explanation.exam_pattern: Awareness programs target behavior change and culture across the workforce.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Security awareness programs

questions.stem: A metric confirms that 100% of critical systems were recovered within their recovery time objectives during the last disaster-recovery test - measuring achievement of a desired goal. This is BEST described as a:

options.text: Key goal indicator (KGI)
Key risk indicator (KRI)
Service level agreement (SLA)
Key performance indicator (KPI)

explanation.correct: A KGI measures whether a goal/outcome was achieved (here, meeting recovery objectives) - it confirms the end result.

distractors.B: A KRI signals rising risk exposure, not achievement of a goal.
distractors.C: An SLA is a contractual service commitment, not a metric type.
distractors.D: A KPI measures how well a process is performing, not whether the goal was met.

explanation.exam_pattern: KGI = goal achieved; KPI = process performance; KRI = risk trend.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Key goal indicators

questions.stem: What MOST makes a security metric valuable to management?

options.text: It produces the largest possible number
It is relevant, measurable, and supports a decision or action
It is highly technical and hard to interpret
Its definition changes every reporting period

explanation.correct: A useful metric is relevant to objectives, measurable, and actionable - it informs a decision; otherwise it is noise.

distractors.A: A big number is not inherently meaningful.
distractors.C: Hard-to-interpret metrics do not support decisions.
distractors.D: Shifting definitions destroy comparability and trust.

explanation.exam_pattern: Good metrics are relevant, measurable, and actionable (decision-supporting).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Characteristics of good metrics

questions.stem: Executives ask the information security manager to justify a proposed control's value. Which is the BEST way to express it?

options.text: The number of hours the team spent installing it
The reduction in expected loss (risk) relative to the control's cost
The brand of the appliance purchased
The number of lines in the firewall configuration

explanation.correct: Value to executives is best expressed in business/financial terms: how much the control reduces expected loss (risk) for its cost - a cost-benefit view they can act on.

distractors.A: Install hours measure effort, not value or risk reduction.
distractors.C: The appliance brand says nothing about value delivered.
distractors.D: Configuration size is a technical detail, not business value.

explanation.exam_pattern: Express value to executives as risk/expected-loss reduction versus cost (cost-benefit).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Communicating security value

questions.stem: Which type of metric is MOST useful to the security operations team for managing day-to-day performance?

options.text: The CEO's travel schedule
Operational metrics such as mean time to detect, mean time to respond, and patch timeliness
The company's quarterly stock price
The board's three-year risk-appetite statement

explanation.correct: Operations teams need granular operational metrics (detection/response times, patch timeliness) to manage and improve day-to-day performance.

distractors.A: The CEO's schedule is irrelevant to operations metrics.
distractors.C: Stock price is unrelated to security operations performance.
distractors.D: A multi-year appetite statement is strategic, not operational.

explanation.exam_pattern: Match the metric to the audience: operations needs operational metrics; the board needs strategic ones.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Audience-appropriate metrics

questions.stem: To make a security metric meaningful for tracking progress, what is MOST important to establish alongside it?

options.text: A rule that the metric may never be changed
A longer report cover page
A new color scheme for the dashboard
A baseline and target/threshold so trends and deviations can be interpreted

explanation.correct: A metric is only interpretable against a baseline and target/threshold; these let you see trends, judge performance, and know when to act.

distractors.A: Metrics may need refinement; freezing definitions forever is not a requirement for meaning.
distractors.B: A cover page adds no analytical value.
distractors.C: Colors are cosmetic, not analytical.

explanation.exam_pattern: Give metrics a baseline and target so trends/deviations are meaningful.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Baselines and targets for metrics

questions.stem: A manager wants to report security performance across several perspectives - financial, customer/stakeholder, internal process, and learning/growth - linked to business goals. Which tool is BEST suited?

options.text: A single packet-capture file
A balanced scorecard
An organization chart
A raw server log

explanation.correct: A balanced scorecard reports performance across multiple linked perspectives tied to strategy, which suits communicating security's contribution to business goals.

distractors.A: A packet capture is a low-level technical artifact, not a strategic reporting tool.
distractors.C: An org chart shows structure, not performance.
distractors.D: A raw log is operational detail, not a multi-perspective scorecard.

explanation.exam_pattern: Multiple linked perspectives tied to strategy = balanced scorecard.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Balanced scorecard for security

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: A metric that measures how well a process is performing against its target, such as the mean time to detect incidents, is a key _____ indicator. (one word)

explanation.correct: A key performance indicator (KPI) measures how well a process performs against a target, such as detection or patching timeliness.
explanation.exam_pattern: KPI = process performance vs target; KGI = goal met; KRI = risk trend.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Key performance indicators

questions.stem: A cloud provider will not permit customer on-site audits. What is the BEST alternative way for the information security manager to gain assurance over the provider's controls?

options.text: Trust the provider's marketing brochure
Skip assurance entirely to save time
Assume the controls are adequate because the provider is large
Obtain and review an independent third-party audit report, such as a SOC 2 Type II

explanation.correct: When direct audits are not possible, an independent assurance report (e.g., SOC 2 Type II) provides credible, third-party evidence of the provider's control design and operating effectiveness.

distractors.A: Marketing material is not independent assurance.
distractors.B: Skipping assurance leaves third-party risk unmanaged.
distractors.C: Size is not evidence of effective controls.

explanation.exam_pattern: No on-site audit? Rely on independent assurance reports (SOC 2 Type II) for evidence.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Third-party assurance reports

questions.stem: Under the cloud shared-responsibility model for infrastructure as a service (IaaS), who is responsible for securing the customer's data and its access configuration?

options.text: No one is responsible
The end users' internet service provider
The customer organization
The cloud provider alone

explanation.correct: In IaaS, the provider secures the underlying infrastructure, but the customer remains responsible for its own data, identity/access configuration, and workloads.

distractors.A: Responsibility is shared and clearly allocated, not absent.
distractors.B: An ISP has no role in securing the customer's cloud data.
distractors.D: The provider secures the infrastructure, not the customer's data and configuration.

explanation.exam_pattern: Shared responsibility: provider secures the infrastructure; customer secures its data, access, and config.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Cloud shared responsibility

questions.stem: A critical vendor subcontracts part of its data processing to other companies. Which risk should the information security manager MOST consider?

options.text: Only the risk that the vendor might raise its prices
The risk that the vendor's logo might change
No additional risk, since it is entirely the vendor's problem
Fourth-party (subcontractor/supply-chain) risk, requiring flow-down security requirements and visibility

explanation.correct: Subcontractors (fourth parties) can introduce risk the organization is still accountable for; contracts should flow down security requirements and provide visibility into the chain.

distractors.A: Pricing is a commercial concern, not the security risk at issue.
distractors.B: A logo change is trivial and irrelevant to data risk.
distractors.C: Accountability extends down the supply chain; it is not solely the vendor's problem.

explanation.exam_pattern: Subcontracting creates fourth-party/supply-chain risk - flow down requirements and keep visibility.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Fourth-party and supply-chain risk

questions.stem: When a contract with a third-party service provider ends, what is the MOST important security action?

options.text: Delete the organization's own production systems
Leave the provider's accounts active in case they are needed later
Immediately publish a public thank-you note
Ensure return or secure destruction of the organization's data and revoke all of the provider's access

explanation.correct: Secure offboarding requires recovering or destroying the organization's data and revoking the provider's access so no residual exposure remains after the relationship ends.

distractors.A: Deleting your own systems is self-harm and unrelated to offboarding the vendor.
distractors.B: Leaving accounts active is an open door - exactly the risk to close.
distractors.C: A thank-you note does nothing to manage the security exposure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Vendor offboarding = recover/destroy data and revoke all access.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Third-party offboarding

questions.stem: With hundreds of third-party relationships, how should the information security manager BEST focus third-party risk-management effort?

options.text: Treat every vendor identically regardless of risk
Review only the vendor with the smallest contract
Tier and prioritize vendors based on the sensitivity of data and level of access they have (risk-based)
Ignore vendors that have been used for a long time

explanation.correct: Risk-based tiering concentrates due diligence and monitoring on the vendors that handle the most sensitive data or have the most access, using limited resources where exposure is greatest.

distractors.A: Identical treatment wastes effort on low-risk vendors and under-serves high-risk ones.
distractors.B: Contract size is not a proxy for risk.
distractors.D: Long-standing vendors are not automatically low risk.

explanation.exam_pattern: Tier/prioritize vendors by data sensitivity and access (risk-based focus).

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Risk-based vendor tiering

questions.stem: Which contractual clause MOST helps the organization meet its OWN breach-notification obligations if a vendor is compromised?

options.text: A clause fixing the vendor's logo colors
A clause waiving all vendor responsibility for incidents
A requirement that the vendor notify the organization of security incidents within a defined timeframe
A clause prohibiting the vendor from ever discussing security

explanation.correct: A defined incident-notification clause ensures the organization learns of a vendor breach quickly enough to meet its own regulatory notification deadlines.

distractors.A: Logo colors are irrelevant to incident notification.
distractors.B: Waiving vendor responsibility removes the very obligation needed.
distractors.D: Prohibiting security discussion is counterproductive and dangerous.

explanation.exam_pattern: Require timely vendor incident notification so you can meet your own breach-notification obligations.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Vendor incident-notification clauses

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Risk introduced to an organization through its vendors, suppliers, and service providers is collectively called third-_____ risk. (one word)

explanation.correct: Third-party risk is the risk arising from vendors, suppliers, and service providers; the organization stays accountable and must assess and monitor it.
explanation.exam_pattern: Third-party risk = risk from vendors/suppliers/providers; accountability stays in-house.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 3 - Third-party risk

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes a security 'event' from a security 'incident'?

options.text: They are identical terms
An event can only occur on weekends
An incident is always less serious than an event
An event is any observable occurrence in a system; an incident is an event (or series) that actually or imminently jeopardizes security or violates policy

explanation.correct: An event is any observable occurrence; it becomes an incident when it adversely affects (or is about to affect) confidentiality, integrity, or availability, or violates policy. Not every event is an incident.

distractors.A: They are related but distinct - the incident is the adverse subset of events.
distractors.B: Timing (weekends) has nothing to do with the definition.
distractors.C: An incident is the more serious, adverse case, not the lesser one.

explanation.exam_pattern: Event = any observable occurrence; incident = an adverse event that harms or threatens security/policy.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 4 - Events versus incidents

questions.stem: To ensure common incident types (such as phishing or malware) are handled consistently and quickly, what should the information security manager develop in advance?

options.text: A larger advertising budget
A company picnic schedule
Incident response playbooks (predefined procedures) for those scenarios
A list of the CEO's favorite restaurants

explanation.correct: Playbooks (runbooks) give responders predefined, repeatable steps for specific incident types, improving speed and consistency when time matters.

distractors.A: An advertising budget does nothing for incident handling.
distractors.B: A picnic schedule is irrelevant to response.
distractors.D: Restaurant preferences have no bearing on readiness.

explanation.exam_pattern: Prepare playbooks/runbooks for common incident types for fast, consistent response.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 4 - Incident response playbooks

questions.stem: Which factor MOST enables a fast, coordinated response when an incident occurs?

options.text: Letting whoever is available improvise each time
A single technician who keeps all knowledge in their head
Waiting for the annual audit to assign duties
Clearly defined roles, responsibilities, and the authority to declare and escalate an incident

explanation.correct: Predefined roles, responsibilities, and clear authority (including who may declare and escalate) let the team act immediately and in a coordinated way under pressure.

distractors.A: Improvising each time yields inconsistent, delayed responses.
distractors.B: Concentrating knowledge in one person creates a single point of failure.
distractors.C: Assigning duties only at audit time is far too slow for incidents.

explanation.exam_pattern: Defined roles and clear authority to declare/escalate drive fast, coordinated response.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 4 - Roles, responsibilities and authority

questions.stem: To ensure specialized forensic and response expertise is available during a major incident, what should the information security manager arrange BEFORE an incident occurs?

options.text: A standing ban on calling any outside experts
A pre-arranged incident response/forensics retainer and defined external contacts
A new marketing campaign
Nothing - such help can always be found instantly mid-incident

explanation.correct: A retainer and predefined external contacts (forensics, legal, law enforcement) ensure expert help can be engaged immediately rather than scrambled for during a crisis.

distractors.A: Banning outside experts removes a valuable response option.
distractors.C: A marketing campaign is unrelated to response readiness.
distractors.D: Finding and contracting experts mid-incident wastes critical time.

explanation.exam_pattern: Arrange IR/forensics retainers and external contacts in advance - readiness is preparation.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 4 - External support and retainers

questions.stem: Which capability MOST improves an organization's ability to DETECT incidents early?

options.text: Disabling logging to save storage space
Reducing the security team to cut costs
Turning off all alerts to avoid noise
Centralized logging and monitoring with tuned alerting (e.g., a SIEM)

explanation.correct: Centralized logging/monitoring with well-tuned alerts gives timely visibility into suspicious activity, which is foundational to early detection.

distractors.A: Disabling logging removes the very data needed to detect incidents.
distractors.B: Cutting the team reduces capacity to detect and respond.
distractors.C: Turning off alerts blinds the team to real events.

explanation.exam_pattern: Early detection depends on monitoring/logging with tuned alerting - not on turning visibility off.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 4 - Detection capability

questions.stem: A company has no incident response capability at all. What is the information security manager's BEST FIRST step to establish one?

options.text: Obtain senior-management support and an approved incident response policy/mandate, then build the plan and team
Plan to personally handle every future incident alone
Wait until the first incident to decide what to do
Immediately buy the most expensive forensic tool on the market

explanation.correct: Like any program element, an IR capability starts with management support and an approved policy/mandate, which provide authority and resources; the plan, team, and tooling follow.

distractors.B: One person handling everything is unsustainable and a single point of failure.
distractors.C: Waiting for an incident is reactive and leaves the organization exposed.
distractors.D: Buying tools first is technology-led and premature without a mandate or plan.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stand up a capability by first securing management support/mandate and policy, then plan/team/tools.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 4 - Establishing an IR capability

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: A documented, step-by-step set of procedures for responding to a specific incident type (also called a runbook) is commonly known as a _____. (one word)

explanation.correct: A playbook (runbook) is a predefined, step-by-step procedure for a specific incident type, enabling fast and consistent response.
explanation.exam_pattern: Playbook/runbook = predefined step-by-step response procedure for a specific scenario.

references: ISACA CISM Review Manual: Domain 4 - Playbooks and runbooks

questions.stem: Which sequence BEST represents the incident response lifecycle?

options.text: Containment -> Preparation -> Lessons learned -> Detection
